title: Types of economic systems and economic resources — 1.2.2

blocks.heading: Market allocation through decisions and prices
blocks.text: A market economic system coordinates production mainly through prices, private ownership and decisions by buyers and sellers. Households make consumption and work choices; producers compare expected revenues with costs. A change in customers' willingness and ability to buy can alter the incentive to supply a product. In an original example, increased paying demand for bicycle repairs could encourage a workshop to extend its service or a rival to enter. The response depends on available workers, equipment and finance; the prospect of revenue does not instantly create those resources. Competition can give customers alternatives and encourage cost control, while private ownership allows owners to decide how their assets are used within the rules that apply. The model describes the main coordinating role of markets, not the absence of every legal or public institution.

blocks.heading: Purchasing power is not identical to need
blocks.text: A market responds to demand backed by purchasing power. A low-income community can have a strong need for a service but limited ability to pay enough to cover its costs. This can leave an access problem even where producers are behaving consistently with their financial incentives. Some wider costs or benefits may also fall on people who are not parties to the transaction. Competition, information and the ability to enter a market affect the outcome. When evaluating market allocation, state the relevant condition instead of assuming that private ownership guarantees low prices or good quality. Compare the incentives with the users' needs and the resources available. Topic 3.5 develops the difference between competitive and monopoly conditions, while topic 6.3 examines reasons for government involvement.

blocks.heading: Planned allocation through public priorities
blocks.text: A planned economic system gives government planning the main role in directing resource allocation and production targets. Public authorities decide priorities, arrange the use of productive resources and can influence prices or the distribution of output. A plan can give weight to goals such as access to essential services or development of an underserved area, including needs that would not generate enough paying demand for private provision. Scarcity still exists. Choosing more resources for one service can reduce the resources available elsewhere. Planning therefore requires a comparison of alternatives rather than merely a statement of desirable goals. In an original example, allocating additional vehicles to a remote service requires funding, workers and equipment that could have served another route. Public ownership does not remove the underlying resource trade-off.

blocks.heading: Information and incentives affect a plan
blocks.text: An authority needs reliable information about demand, costs and available resources. A fixed production target can become unsuitable when needs or supply conditions change. If information travels slowly or managers have little incentive to respond, shortages, unwanted output or avoidable costs may result. These are risks to explain, not proof that every public activity performs poorly. Monitoring, local knowledge and accountability can improve implementation. Evaluate whether the particular planning arrangement can obtain the needed information and respond to it. Compare its ability to deliver access or coordination with the resources used and alternatives forgone. A judgement about a transport route, for example, should consider service coverage, operating constraints and performance, rather than substituting a general slogan about government control.

blocks.heading: Mixed allocation combines arrangements
blocks.text: A mixed economic system combines private market decisions with government provision, ownership or regulation. Privately operated shops may coexist with public services, while rules influence how private businesses behave. The label does not mean that government and private activity must each account for half of production. The balance can vary across countries and industries. A mixed arrangement can retain incentives for customer responsiveness while using public action to address gaps or wider effects. For an invented town's waste collection, private operation might be combined with service standards and public funding for households unable to afford a full fee. Identify the actual responsibilities: who owns the equipment, chooses the service area, pays for it and checks the result. The mixture's design matters more than the label alone.

blocks.heading: Judge the combination rather than the name
blocks.text: A mixed arrangement can face problems from either weak market incentives or weak public implementation. A poorly designed contract may give an operator little reason to maintain quality; unclear rules can make accountability difficult. Conversely, a well-specified service obligation with credible monitoring may improve coverage. Compare efficiency, access and responsiveness in the circumstances described. Explain how each expected benefit could arise and a limitation that might prevent it. A supported conclusion identifies which combination is appropriate for the stated objective and resources. It need not claim that one system is best for every activity. This connects the classification of systems to the later study of government policies, while retaining the scarcity and opportunity-cost reasoning introduced in topic 1.1. A change in one policy does not establish that the whole economy has changed system; identify the coordinating arrangements across the activities being considered.
